text: My friends thought I was broke.
The couch in my studio had a tear in the left cushion,
and I hid it under a blanket from Target.
My TV was a refurbished 32-inch that cost $89.
My car had a crack in the windshield
that I ignored for two months.
I was 23 years old, eating rice and black beans
out of a $3 pot from Goodwill.
Then one night, I opened my brokerage app.
The balance said $61,412.
Nobody in my life knew that number existed.
And before this year ends, it will cross $100,000.
Before 2027 even begins,
let me be clear about where it came from.
No inheritance.
No lottery, no startup sale, no lucky crypto bet.
I left college with $9,000 in student debt
and a $55,000 job from a career fair.
My parents covered part of my tuition,
and I'm grateful for that.
But after graduation, I was on my own.
What I had was 20 habits, boring ones.
Habits that looked like struggling from the outside.
And I'm gonna give you all 20 with the real numbers
because every one of them is something
you can start this week.
Habit one, I automated my investing
before I could touch the money.
On the 15th and the 30th of every month,
$750 left my checking account
and went into my 401k and a Roth IRA.
I set it up in my first week at the company.
My brain simply learned to live on what was left.
Automation isn't about convenience.
It removes the decision,
and the decision is where most people lose.
Habit two, I tracked every dollar in a paper notebook.
Every night, five minutes, three columns, needs, wants, bills.
The first month exposed over $300 I had noticed.
Forgotten subscriptions, vending machines,
a gas station, sparkling water habit
that cost me about $80 a month.
The notebook cost $3, habit three.
My batch cooked every Sunday.
Two hours, three big meals, a pot of chili,
a tray of roasted chicken and vegetables,
a large batch of rice with whatever protein was on sale.
That covered most of my week.
My groceries came to about $220 a month.
Friends who ate out and ordered delivery
were spending nearly double.
That gap, 3,000 a year, becomes roughly $340,000
over 30 years at 8%.
Habit four, I kept rent under a quarter of my take home pay.
My studio cost $730.
No granite counters, no in-unit laundry.
It had a working stove and a door that locked.
My friends paid 11 to 1400 in trendier neighborhoods.
That $500 monthly gap invested for 20 years
is about $295,000.
Habit five, I bought a used car with cash,
a 2014 Honda Civic, $8,200 from a private seller.
Before buying, I paid a mechanic $75 to inspect it
and that inspection saved me from two other cars
with hidden problems.
Oil every 5,000 miles, tires rotated twice a year.
Herely maintenance averaged about $600.
No car payment.
My total cost to own that car,
including insurance and gas, was around 3,400 a year.
A typical new car owner spends several times that.
Invested, the difference passes a million dollars
over a working lifetime.
Habit six, I used the library for everything.
Books, movies and through the Libby app,
audio books for my commute.
Two books a month, $0 and it changed something deeper.
Once you learn you can use something without owning it,
you start questioning ownership everywhere else.
Habit seven, I made coffee at home five days a week
and bought one on Fridays.
That Friday coffee was my ritual,
550 from a local shop.
Total coffee cost for the year,
including beans and a $12 French press was about $290.
A daily coffee shop habit runs 1,500 or more.
The difference invested for 20 years
comes close to $60,000.
Habit eight, I never paid for a gym.
I ran outside and followed a free YouTube body weight program.
I used pull up bar from Craig's list,
cost $15 and a jump rope cost eight.
Gym memberships run $40 to $60 a month
and most people go only a few times.
My $60 went to my Roth IRA instead.
Over 25 years, that's roughly $53,000.
A pull up bar and a jump rope, habit nine.
I negotiated every recurring bill once a year.
Carrying insurance, phone, internet.
I called, said I was thinking of switching
and asked what they could do.
All three dropped.
Total savings, about $480 a year
from less than 30 minutes on the phone.
Nobody's side hustle pays that well per hour.
Habit 10, I spent discretionary money in cash only.
Every two weeks I took out $200,
dining out, entertainment, personal items.
All of it came from that one envelope.
When the cash ran out,
I was done until the next paycheck.
Physical money makes spending hurt
in a way a card swipe never does.
It wasn't willpower, it was architecture.
10 habits down.
But the next 10 are where the real acceleration happened
because I'm about to show you the one habit
that gave me free money from my employer
and the one mistake I almost made
that could have erased all of it.
Habit 11, I bought almost everything secondhand.
My entire apartment, furniture, kitchen, electronics
cost me under $900 through Goodwill,
Facebook Marketplace and a neighbor's moving sale.
A coworker with a similar apartment
furnished hers for over 6,000.
I kept the same logic with my phone.
I used a refurbished one for $260
and kept it for three and a half years.
I made calls, ran every app I needed
and saved me thousands compared to upgrading every cycle.
Habit 12, I waited 24 hours before any purchase over $30
and I did the math on the big ones.
See something I want?
Wait one day.
If I still wanted it tomorrow, I bought it.
Most of the time, the urge died overnight.
And when something was truly tempting,
I ran the shadow price.
A $280 concert ticket isn't $280.
At 8% over 40 years, it's about 6,000.
I still said yes to some things,
but now every yes was a deliberate trade,
so I never felt guilty.
Habit 13, I unsubscribed from every marketing email
the moment it arrived.
Each one is built by a team
whose job is to make you spend money you didn't plan to.
Within three months, my inbox was quiet.
You can't be tempted by what you never see.
Habit 14, I deleted every shopping app from my phone.
If I wanted something, I had to open my laptop,
go to the website and type it in.
Those extra 30 seconds killed a large share
of my online purchases.
I never bought anything from a push notification again.
Now I know what some of you are thinking.
This sounds like two years in a dark apartment
while everyone else lived.
That's not what happened.
I still went to dinner with friends.
Once or twice a month,
and I ordered the $14 dish instead of the $38 one.
I took a Smoky Mountains road trip
that cost $312 total.
I played pickup basketball, hiked,
cooked big weekend meals for fun.
The life was full.
It was just cheap.
Habit 15, I captured the full employer match on day one.
My company matched 100% of the first 3%
and 50% of the next two.
I contributed 5% to 55,000
and my employer added about $2,200 a year.
Free money for checking one box.
Skipping it means turning down part of your pay.
Habit 16, I opened a Roth IRA in my first month
and funded it monthly.
The 2026 limit is $7,500, so about 625 a month.
It went into a total stock market index fund
with a 0.03% expense ratio.
No stock picking, no timing, no influencers.
I bought the whole market every month
and good news and bad and let compounding do the work.
Habit 17, I kept my emergency fund
in a high yield savings account.
4% to 5% versus the national average of under half a percent.
On $5,000, that's about 200 a year instead of 19.
Same money, same access.
Different container.
I built a $7,000 cushion this way
and it protected my investments from every surprise.
Habit 18, I made free entertainment my default.
Parks, trails, library events, free museum days,
movie nights at friends' departments, a deck of cards.
The best evenings of my early 20s
happened in living rooms.
The worst happened at crowded bars
where I spent $80 to have conversations I couldn't hear.
Because paid fund became rare, it felt special.
Habit 19, I treated every windfall as an investment fuel.
My first tax refund was $1,900.
Birthday money added about 300.
One freelance project paid 600.
All of it went straight to the brokerage account.
Money from a refund compounds exactly
like money from a paycheck.
The only difference is how guilty
you feel spending each one.
I deleted that difference.
Habit 20, I read it.
I ran a zero-based budget every month.
Every dollar got a job before the month began.
Groceries, $2,200.
Insurance, $1,800.
Internet, $4,500.
Cash envelope, $4,000.
Investments, $1,500 later, $2,000 after my raise.
Anything left over went to investing.
The budget wasn't a cage.
It was a map, so where did $100,000 actually come from?
About $82,000 was money I put in,
including my employer's match and that emergency fund.
The remaining $18,000 was market growth.
Not a big salary, not a lucky pick.
Mostly just a savings rate near 50%,
kept up for three years,
while the average American saves under five.
That gap isn't about income, it's behavior.
And not one of these habits required earning more.
I remember birthday dinner about 14 months in.
Everyone ordered cocktails and appetizers.
I ordered water and the cheapest entree.
A friend leaned over and asked, half joking,
are you okay?
Do you need money?
I had more invested than anyone at that table.
I just smiled and said I was fine.
Well, built quietly doesn't need an audience.
The balance is the proof,
and at 24 with $100,000 invested,
the math gets interesting.
Left alone at 10% average returns,
that seed grows past $3 million by 65.
But here's what I learned.
Hitting this number is only the first mile.
Every decade after it has its own traps
and most people only see them
once they've already stepped in.
The habits got me here.
Seeing the next turn before I reach it
is what keeps the curve bending.
